transcript: Offcut gives people and browser agents the same cutting stock workbench. Fourteen parts fit, the longboard stays protected. These illustrative measurements cover usable stock, parts, kerf, and the reusable remnant threshold. People own measurements and protection. Registered tools cannot change them. The right-hand panel is an external model recording harness, not a chatbot inside the website. site. A real model chooses native WebM, CP calls on the shared committed workbench. This is not a chat GPT recording. The model compares three complete alternatives, less stock, fewer boards, or useful offcuts. The deterministic branch and bounce solver checks quantities, stock, and one curve per part. A search limit is not a proof of optimality. Less stock and fewer boards, both open 7.2m across 3 boards, 42mm of sawdust, plus 158mm of short scrap. Keeping useful offcuts opens 10.08m across 6 boards, 42mm of sawdust, no short scrap, and 3.038m reusable. useable. Computed trade-offs not measured time or carbon savings. The agent inspects and stages the exact plan. Pause for review. This is not approval. Check stock identities, quantities, and kerf. No registered tool can approve. These UI controls are automated, not proof of human presence. Now the controls check the acknowledgement. Then, they click approve cut sheet. The model inspects approval and exports the actual CSV, 14 parts part identifiers, offsets, kerf, and the exact approved plan identifier. Another draft cannot inherit approval. Typing four leaves committed kerf at three. Pending edits block staging without moving focus or saving. Now commit. Revision two invalidates the old approval. The old plan is stale. The model replans, 14 parts, 56 mm of sawdust. Revision 2 is staged, not approved. The acknowledgment stays unchecked. Offcut itself needs no account. Model Key or McKend. A workbench and MIT license source are public. These are planning estimates, not machine instructions. Barify usable stock and safe cutting conditions at the bench.
